A2.2 Network Architecture

Topic A2: Networks | Devices, Addresses & Models

Retrieval Practice

Recall A2.1 (Network Fundamentals) before we build the architecture.

  1. What’s the difference between a LAN and a WAN?
  2. Why might edge computing reduce latency?
  3. What does “fault tolerance” mean in a distributed system?

Press Down for answers

Answer 1

What’s the difference between a LAN and a WAN?

A LAN covers a small area (building/campus). A WAN connects LANs over large distances.

Answer 2

Why might edge computing reduce latency?

Because data is processed closer to the user/source, reducing travel time across the network.

Answer 3

What does “fault tolerance” mean in a distributed system?

The system can keep working even when some components/nodes fail.

The Big Question

🤔 You press “Print” and the right printer responds.

You open a website and it leaves your home network.

How does traffic know where to go?

❌ Misconception: “Wi‑Fi just broadcasts everything to everyone.”

Modern networks direct traffic using addresses and specialised devices.

✅ Key idea: different devices make decisions at different layers.

Inside a LAN, switching uses MAC addresses. Between networks, routing uses IP addresses.

The Hardware Stack (Who does what?)

Which device should handle each job: translate, connect, route, or switch?

Modem: analogue ↔ digital conversion (ISP link ↔ router)

Router: chooses paths between networks using IP addresses

Switch: directs traffic within a LAN using MAC addresses

Gateway: translates between different protocols/systems

Switch vs Router

Why do we need both a switch and a router in real networks?

Switch (within a LAN)

Forwards frames to the correct port based on MAC addresses.

Efficient local delivery: your laptop → printer.

Router (between networks)

Forwards packets between networks using IP addresses and routing tables.

Enables your LAN to reach the internet.

🧠 Quick Check

Which device directs traffic within a network segment using MAC addresses?

Switch — local delivery inside a LAN.

Networking Models

Should one powerful machine serve everyone — or should everyone share?

Client–Server

Centralised control: server provides, client requests.

Risk: single point of failure if server goes down.

Peer‑to‑Peer (P2P)

Decentralised: nodes share resources directly.

Use: file sharing, some blockchain designs.

Client–Server vs P2P (Trade-offs)

Which model scales best, and which is easiest to manage?
AspectClient–ServerP2P
ControlCentralisedDistributed
ReliabilityServer is a critical pointNo single server, but harder coordination
SecurityEasier to manage centrallyMore complex trust/verification
Typical examplesWebsites, email serversBitTorrent, some blockchain networks

🧠 Quick Check

Traditional web browsing (loading pages from a website) is usually which model?

Client–server — your browser (client) requests resources from a web server.

Misconception Check

A. Routers use MAC addresses to forward traffic between networks.

B. Switches are mainly for directing traffic inside a LAN.

C. Client–server has no single point of failure.

D. A gateway can translate between different protocols.

Press Down for answers

Answers

A: False. Routers use IP addresses; switches use MAC addresses.

B: True. Switches forward frames within a network segment.

C: False. The server can be a critical failure point.

D: True. Gateways connect disparate systems by translation.

Key Takeaways

  • Different devices serve different roles: modem, switch, router, gateway.
  • Switching is local (MAC); routing is between networks (IP).
  • Architectures differ: client–server vs P2P, each with trade-offs.
